items.title: Driving after Epilepsy Surgery
items.summary: Chance of a seizure with impaired awareness in the next year after epilepsy surgery, for people who are seizure-free or still have auras only.
details: 819 patients operated at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, London (1990–2014), with 9307 graded patient-years.
Seizure-free for 1, 2 or 3 years: 4.9%, 3.5% and 2.4%. Auras only over the same periods: 11.3%, 9.2% and 7.8%.
Every combination is shown with its 95% confidence interval, next to the 20% and 2% orientation cut-offs used in some driving rules.

calcs.name: Driving after Epilepsy Surgery
calcs.desc: Chance of a seizure with impaired awareness in the next year after epilepsy surgery, for people who are seizure-free or have auras only.
calcs.outcome: Chance of a seizure with impaired awareness in the next 12 months (COSY) after epilepsy surgery, by the worst ILAE outcome grade over the previous 1, 2 or 3 years.

cite.authors: Fairclough S, O'Keeffe AG, de Tisi J, Duncan JS

calcs.rationale: Large single-centre surgical cohort (n=819, 9307 graded patient-years, up to 25 years, NHNN London) giving robust-SE GEE estimates of next-year risk by ILAE grade over the previous 1-3 years; descriptive conditional risks, not externally validated, and auras are self-reported.
calcs.rec_why: Recommended — clinically useful with good evidence (tier B, n=819).

items.title: Brain metastases: first prospective seizure data after radiosurgery
items.summary: Interim results of the SAFER study, 75 patients treated with stereotactic radiosurgery, added as context to our two brain-metastasis calculators.
details: 8 of 75 patients (10.7%, 95% CI 4.7–19.9) had a seizure within 12 months; 9.2% were new-onset seizures.
Of those seizure-free at 6 months, 5.8% had a seizure by 12 months, and no first seizure occurred after month 9.
This is an interim analysis of 75 of 375 planned patients with no risk-factor model, so it neither validates nor refutes either calculator.

sources.cite: de Boisanger J, et al. Clin Oncol 2026;57:104222

calcs.name: BMERS
calcs.desc: Epilepsy risk in patients with brain metastases.
calcs.outcome: Risk factors for the development of epilepsy in patients with brain metastases

cite.authors: Wolpert F, Lareida A, Terziev R, et al.

calcs.rationale: Reasonable-sized single-centre retrospective derivation (n=799, 226 epilepsy events) yielding a 0-8 points score with AUC 0.75, but only post-hoc internal confirmation and no independent external validation.
calcs.rec_why: Recommended — clinically useful with good evidence (tier B, n=799).

calcs.name: Brain Metastases Seizures
calcs.desc: Probability of a seizure in a patient with brain metastases, from 3 factors (small cohort).
calcs.outcome: Probability of developing a seizure in a patient with brain metastases, from 3 factors (single static estimate)

cite.authors: Makkawi S, Alqurashi RM, Aljabri A, et al.

calcs.rationale: Single-centre retrospective cohort of 272 patients (80 seizure events) with only internal bootstrap validation (AUC 0.82) and no independent external validation, so preliminary.

items.title: Glioma surgery: how often do seizures follow?
items.summary: Two new studies show the overall size of postoperative seizure risk, added as context to our glioma calculators.
details: SPRING trial, 94 seizure-naive adults: about one in three had a first seizure within 12 months, with or without levetiracetam prophylaxis. The trial closed early and was underpowered.
Glioblastoma, 39 Japanese centres, 1099 patients: 26% had a late postoperative seizure, at a mean of 194 days after surgery.
Neither study is a prediction model; both are shown as reference points only.

sources.cite: Jenkinson MD, et al. Neuro-Oncol Pract (online 2025)
Inoue A, et al. Neuro-Oncol Adv 2026;8:vdag205

calcs.name: Glioma-Related Epilepsy
calcs.desc: Epilepsy in diffuse high-grade glioma.
calcs.outcome: Glioma-related epilepsy in patients with diffuse high-grade glioma after the 2016 WHO update: seizure characteristics, risk factors, and clinical outcomes

cite.authors: Li L, Fang S, Li G, et al.

calcs.rationale: Single-centre (Beijing Tiantan) retrospective cohort of 449 high-grade glioma patients reporting predictor odds ratios with no internal or external validation of a formal model.

calcs.name: PGREM
calcs.desc: Post-operative glioma-related epilepsy risk.
calcs.outcome: Development of an integrated predictive model for postoperative glioma-related epilepsy using gene-signature and clinical data

cite.authors: Li L, Zhang C, Wang Z, et al.

calcs.rationale: Retrospective single-centre (Beijing Tiantan) study, n=208 split into training 166/validation 42 with only internal random-split validation and requiring tumour RNA-seq; authors themselves flag small sample and need for external validation.

items.title: Drug Resistance at Diagnosis (children)
items.summary: Probability that a child with newly diagnosed epilepsy will develop drug-resistant epilepsy, from eight features available at diagnosis.
details: 4208 children from a single tertiary centre in Seoul, followed to 2024; 33.7% developed drug-resistant epilepsy.
AUC 0.778 in a held-out validation set (optimism-corrected 0.761), with good calibration.
Internal validation only, and a referral population, so absolute risks may be higher than in general practice.

calcs.name: Drug Resistance at Diagnosis (children)
calcs.desc: Probability that a child with newly diagnosed epilepsy develops drug-resistant epilepsy, from eight features known at diagnosis.
calcs.outcome: Probability that a child with newly diagnosed epilepsy develops drug-resistant epilepsy, from eight features known at diagnosis.

cite.authors: Kwon O, Nam YS, Kim HJ, Yeh HR, Kim MJ, Lee YJ, Kim E, Lee EH, You SJ, Ko TS, Yum MS

calcs.rationale: Large single-centre tertiary cohort (n=4208, 1419 DRE events) with LASSO-selected logistic model; AUC 0.778 (95% CI 0.751-0.805) in a held-out random 30% split, optimism-corrected 0.761, good calibration (slope 1.06). Validation is internal only (same-centre random split), and the 33.7% DRE rate reflects tertiary referral, so tier B. Only model on the site predicting general paediatric drug resistance at diagnosis; the authors publish a matching calculator, and our page reproduces their worked example (76.2%).
calcs.rec_why: Recommended — large derivation cohort (n=4208) and the only model for drug resistance at diagnosis in children, but tier B: single tertiary centre, internal validation only.

items.title: Seizure Freedom after Focal Resection (children)
items.summary: Chance that a child stays seizure-free 1 and 2 years after focal or lobar resection, from five features known at the first postoperative review.
details: 256 children aged 1–18 years from one centre, 90 recurrences.
C-index 0.81 after bootstrap correction and 0.79 in a later temporal validation cohort.
No external validation yet.

calcs.name: Seizure Freedom after Focal Resection (children)
calcs.desc: Chance of staying seizure-free 1 and 2 years after focal or lobar resection in children, from five features known at the first postoperative review.
calcs.outcome: Chance of staying seizure-free 1 and 2 years after focal or lobar resection in children, from five clinical, surgical, histopathological and EEG features known at the first postoperative review.

cite.authors: Dong X, Sun T

calcs.rationale: Single-centre paediatric cohort (n=256; 181 training / 75 temporal validation, 90 recurrences) with LASSO-selected Cox model; bootstrap-corrected C 0.81 and 0.79 in a same-centre temporal cohort applied without recalibration. No external validation, and the >38 spikes/h cut-off was derived in this cohort, so tier B. Only model on the site for seizure freedom after focal resection in children (Jehi is adult and preoperative; HOPS is hemispheric surgery).
calcs.rec_why: Recommended — the only model for seizure freedom after focal resection in children, but tier B: single centre (n=256), validated only in a later cohort from the same centre.

items.title: Seizure/Epilepsy Risk Score (PICU)
items.summary: For critically ill children with acute symptomatic seizures or encephalopathy: the chance of a later seizure or epilepsy diagnosis after discharge.
details: A 0–4 point score from developmental delay, seizures before and during continuous EEG, and epileptiform discharges.
Observed risk rises from 13% at score 0 to 71–96% at scores 1–4.
Single-centre prospective cohort from the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia PICU.

calcs.name: Seizure/Epilepsy Risk Score (PICU)
calcs.desc: Later seizure or epilepsy diagnosis after acute symptomatic seizures in critically ill children, from 4 clinical and continuous-EEG items.
calcs.outcome: Subsequent seizure or epilepsy diagnosis after acute symptomatic seizures in the PICU, from four clinical and continuous-EEG items.

cite.authors: Abend NS, Fung FW, Parikh DS, Ramos M, Xiao R, Topjian AA

calcs.rationale: Single-centre prospective PICU cohort (CHOP, n=365 with follow-up, 234 events); AUC 0.81 is apparent (derivation cohort only) with no internal or external validation, the outcome is an ICD-10 code at variable follow-up and the follow-up subset was enriched for higher-risk children; the authors state it needs external validation. Only paediatric acute-symptomatic tool on the site (complements adult EPI-PASS, also tier C).

items.title: New section: status epilepticus
items.summary: Nine tools on mortality, functional outcome and later epilepsy after status epilepticus, including the ACARD score for 30-day mortality.
details: ACARD (Neurology 2026) was externally validated in Salzburg (AUC 0.845) and outperformed STESS, mSTESS, EMSE and SACE; it is our editor's choice for short-term mortality.
The ACD score covers 2-year mortality, and the Alanís-Bernal curves show 5-year survival by group.
Also included: STESS, EMSE, END-IT, STEPSS (children), AFTER and a Thai national mortality score.

calcs.name: ACARD Score — 30-day Mortality after Status Epilepticus
calcs.desc: Risk of death within 30 days of status epilepticus from 5 routine factors (age, consciousness, aetiology, refractoriness, disability) — externally validated (Lattanzi 2026).
calcs.outcome: Risk of death within 30 days of the onset of non-hypoxic status epilepticus, from the Age–Consciousness–Aetiology–Refractoriness–Disability (ACARD) score.

cite.authors: Lattanzi S, Trinka E, Bosque-Varela P, et al., Meletti S

calcs.rationale: Derived in 689 SE episodes (Modena) and externally validated in an independent multinational cohort (569 episodes, Salzburg) with excellent, well-retained discrimination (AUC 0.864 derivation, 0.845 validation) and good calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.29/0.85). Directly outperformed STESS, mSTESS, EMSE and SACE for 30-day mortality across both convulsive SE and NCSE. Point table + per-score risks taken from the paper (exact, not digitized). The best available tool for short-term (30-day) mortality after status epilepticus.
calcs.rec_why: Editor’s choice for short-term (30-day) mortality after status epilepticus — the strongest available tool for this question (tier A; derived n=689, externally validated n=569, AUC 0.86/0.85; outperforms STESS/mSTESS/EMSE/SACE). Point table and per-score risks are exact from the paper. (For long-term 2-year mortality, see the ACD score.)

calcs.name: ACD Score — Mortality after Status Epilepticus
calcs.desc: Two-year mortality after non-anoxic status epilepticus from the Age–Consciousness–Duration (ACD) score (Roberg 2022; validated Alanís-Bernal 2026).
calcs.outcome: Two-year mortality after an episode of non-anoxic status epilepticus, from the Age–Consciousness–Duration (ACD) score (Roberg 2022 nomogram).

cite.authors: Roberg LE, Monsson O, Kristensen SB, et al., Beier CP

calcs.rationale: ACD score derived in a Danish cohort (n=261; subset n=145 with non/less-damaging causes) and externally validated in independent German (n=906) and Norwegian (n=139) cohorts, with acceptable transported discrimination (AUC 0.69-0.76, best in non-brain-damaging causes) and an almost linear score-mortality relationship (Pearson r2=0.848). Further externally validated for 5-year mortality by Alanís-Bernal 2026 (AUC 0.72). The only tool for mortality after status epilepticus. Note: per-score 2-year mortality here is read from the published nomogram (extraction pending human review).
calcs.rec_why: Recommended — the only tool for mortality after status epilepticus. The ACD score is externally validated across Denmark, Germany and Norway (Roberg 2022) and again in Spain (Alanís-Bernal 2026). Per-score 2-year mortality is read from the published nomogram; pending human review of the extraction (would otherwise be Editor’s choice as the sole tier-A tool for this question).

calcs.name: Survival Curves after Status Epilepticus (5-year)
calcs.desc: Cumulative 5-year mortality after status epilepticus by ACD band and by Lattanzi aetiology — digitized Kaplan–Meier curves (Alanís-Bernal 2026).
calcs.outcome: Cumulative mortality over 5 years after non-anoxic status epilepticus, by ACD score band and by Lattanzi aetiological category.

cite.authors: Alanís-Bernal M, Campos-Fernández D, Abraira L, et al., Santamarina E

calcs.rationale: Descriptive single-centre 5-year survival analysis (n=786) — reference curves, not a validated prediction model: it reports observed mortality by ACD band and Lattanzi aetiology, with no external validation of these stratified estimates. Useful for counselling context alongside the ACD score calculator. Lattanzi/overall 5-year endpoints are exact from the paper; per-band curve shapes are figure-digitized (unreviewed).

calcs.name: STESS — Status Epilepticus Severity Score
calcs.desc: The most validated bedside score for survival after status epilepticus: 4 pre-treatment items (Rossetti 2008). Favorable 0–2 vs unfavorable 3–6.
calcs.outcome: In-hospital survival vs death after an episode of status epilepticus, from four pre-treatment predictors (age, history of seizures, worst seizure type, level of consciousness).

cite.authors: Rossetti AO, Logroscino G, Milligan TA, Michaelides C, Ruffieux C, Bromfield EB

calcs.name: EMSE — 30-day mortality nomogram
calcs.desc: Individualised 30-day mortality after status epilepticus from aetiology, age, comorbidity and EEG — the EMSE-parameter nomogram (Brigo/Meletti 2022, AUC 0.83).
calcs.outcome: Individual probability of 30-day mortality after status epilepticus, from the EMSE parameters (aetiology, EEG, age, comorbidity) re-fitted into a logistic nomogram.

cite.authors: Brigo F, Turcato G, Lattanzi S, Orlandi N, Giovannini G, Zaboli A, Meletti S

calcs.name: END-IT — functional outcome after CSE
calcs.desc: Risk of poor functional outcome (mRS 3–6) at 3 months after convulsive status epilepticus, from 5 bedside items (Gao 2016). Cut-off ≥3.
calcs.outcome: Risk of an unfavorable functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale 3–6, i.e. death or dependence) at 3 months after discharge, in adults with convulsive status epilepticus.

cite.authors: Gao Q, Ou-Yang T-P, Sun X-L, Yang F, Wu C, Kang T, Kang X-G, Jiang W

calcs.name: STEPSS — paediatric SE severity score
calcs.desc: Risk of poor outcome (POPC ≥3) in children with status epilepticus — the paediatric STESS (Sidharth 2019). Cut-off >3.
calcs.outcome: Risk of an unfavourable short-term outcome (Paediatric Overall Performance Category ≥3, i.e. moderate disability to death, at discharge) in children with status epilepticus.

cite.authors: Sidharth, Sankhyan N, Malhi P, Jayashree M

calcs.name: AFTER — epilepsy after status epilepticus
calcs.desc: Risk of developing epilepsy in the 5 years after a de novo status epilepticus, from 4 clinical/EEG items (Rodrigo-Gisbert 2023). Cut-off ≥2.
calcs.outcome: Risk of developing epilepsy (a first unprovoked/remote seizure meeting ILAE criteria) within 5 years after a de novo episode of status epilepticus, in adults with no prior epilepsy.

cite.authors: Rodrigo-Gisbert M, Toledo M, Santamarina E, et al.

calcs.name: SE Mortality Score (national database)
calcs.desc: Purely clinical mortality risk after status epilepticus (age, comorbidities, complications) — no EEG/imaging needed (Tiamkao 2018, n>10,000).
calcs.outcome: Risk of death (in hospital or within 30 days) after status epilepticus, from a clinical risk score built on age, comorbidities and SE complications — no EEG or imaging needed.

cite.authors: Tiamkao S, Pranbul S, Sawanyawisuth K, Thepsuthammarat K, Integrated Epilepsy Research Group

items.title: Six models from epilepsypredictiontools.info
items.summary: Prediction models from UMC Utrecht, now hosted here with the authors' agreement: childhood epilepsy after a first event, withdrawal after paediatric surgery, cognitive outcome after surgery and JME withdrawal.
details: Ported from the authors' own published implementation rather than re-read from figures.
Each model's About panel credits and links the original tool at epilepsypredictiontools.info.

calcs.name: First Seizure in Children — Epilepsy Diagnosis
calcs.desc: Probability of an epilepsy diagnosis in a child after one or more paroxysmal events, from 11 clinical features + EEG.
calcs.outcome: Probability that a child presenting after one or more paroxysmal events will be diagnosed with epilepsy, from 11 clinical features and the interictal EEG available at the first consultation

cite.authors: van Diessen E, Lamberink HJ, Otte WM, Doornebal N, Brouwer OF, Jansen FE, Braun KPJ

calcs.rationale: Developed in 451 children and externally validated in an independent cohort (n=187) with excellent discrimination (AUC 0.86, 95% CI 0.80-0.92; PPV 0.93, NPV 0.76). Retains useful discrimination (AUC 0.73) in the diagnostically uncertain subgroup where it matters most. The only model for this question in children.
calcs.rec_why: Editor's choice — strongest available evidence for this question (tier A, n=451, externally validated in an independent cohort of 187; AUC 0.86). The only model for epilepsy diagnosis in children after paroxysmal events.

calcs.name: Postoperative Relapse after ASM Withdrawal in Children
calcs.desc: Seizure recurrence (2 & 5 yr), long-term seizure freedom and cure after stopping ASM in children who had epilepsy surgery — TimeToStop nomograms.
calcs.outcome: Individualised risk of seizure recurrence (2 and 5 years), chance of long-term seizure freedom, and chance of cure after withdrawal of antiseizure medication following epilepsy surgery in children.

cite.authors: Lamberink HJ, Boshuisen K, Otte WM, Geleijns K, Braun KPJ, on behalf of the TimeToStop Study Group

calcs.rationale: Large multicentre paediatric cohort (766 children, 15 centres, 8 countries) and the only tool for ASM withdrawal after epilepsy surgery in children. Downgraded to B: discrimination is modest (adjusted c 0.68 for recurrence, 0.73 for eventual freedom) and the nomograms were internally (optimism-)adjusted, not validated in an external cohort.
calcs.rec_why: Recommended — the only tool for ASM withdrawal after epilepsy surgery in children (n=766, 15 centres, 8 countries). Tier B: internally adjusted only, not externally validated, and discrimination is modest (c 0.68-0.73). WAMS is the editor's choice for this question overall.

calcs.name: Cognitive Outcome after Surgery — IQ > 85
calcs.desc: Probability of an IQ above 85 two years after paediatric epilepsy surgery, from pre-surgical IQ, resection extent and invasive diagnostics.
calcs.outcome: Probability of post-operative IQ > 85

cite.authors: Cloppenborg T, van Schooneveld MMJ, Hagemann A, Hopf JL, Kalbhenn T, Otte WM, Polster T, Bien CG, Braun KPJ

calcs.rationale: Developed in the Bielefeld/Bethel cohort (n=258) and externally validated in the Utrecht cohort (n=102) with high accuracy (0.82) and excellent discrimination (AUC 0.90, 95% CI 0.84-0.96). The only model predicting intellectual outcome at this threshold in children.
calcs.rec_why: Editor's choice — strongest available evidence for this question (tier A, n=258, externally validated in 102; accuracy 0.82, AUC 0.90).

calcs.name: Cognitive Outcome after Surgery — IQ > 70
calcs.desc: Probability of an IQ above 70 two years after paediatric epilepsy surgery, from pre-surgical IQ and resection extent.
calcs.outcome: Probability of post-operative IQ > 70

cite.authors: Cloppenborg T, van Schooneveld MMJ, Hagemann A, Hopf JL, Kalbhenn T, Otte WM, Polster T, Bien CG, Braun KPJ

calcs.rationale: Developed in the Bielefeld/Bethel cohort (n=258) and externally validated in the Utrecht cohort (n=102) with high accuracy (0.84) and excellent discrimination (AUC 0.92, 95% CI 0.87-0.97). The only model predicting intellectual outcome at this threshold in children.
calcs.rec_why: Editor's choice — strongest available evidence for this question (tier A, n=258, externally validated in 102; accuracy 0.84, AUC 0.92).

calcs.name: Cognitive Outcome after Surgery — DQ > 50
calcs.desc: For children with developmental delay: probability of a developmental quotient above 50 two years after epilepsy surgery.
calcs.outcome: Probability of post-operative DQ > 50

cite.authors: Cloppenborg T, van Schooneveld MMJ, Hagemann A, Hopf JL, Kalbhenn T, Otte WM, Polster T, Bien CG, Braun KPJ

calcs.rationale: The only tool for developmental outcome after epilepsy surgery in children with developmental delay. Downgraded to B relative to its IQ siblings from the same paper: developed in a small cohort (n=127) with 10-fold cross-validation only — no external cohort — and lower correct classification (76%).
calcs.rec_why: Recommended — the only tool for developmental outcome in children with developmental delay. Tier B: small cohort (n=127), 10-fold cross-validation only, correct classification 76% — weaker than its IQ siblings from the same paper.

calcs.name: JME — Post-Withdrawal Relapse Risk
calcs.desc: For someone with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy who is seizure-free: risk of recurrence 2 and 5 years after stopping medication.
calcs.outcome: Individualised risk of seizure recurrence at 2 and 5 years after withdrawal of antiseizure medication in a currently seizure-free person with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME).

cite.authors: Stevelink R, Al-Toma D, Jansen FE, Lamberink HJ, Asadi-Pooya AA, Farazdaghi M, et al., Otte WM, Braun KPJ

calcs.rationale: Individual-participant-data meta-analysis (24 studies) with internal-external (leave-one-cohort-out) cross-validation, c-statistic 0.70 (95% CI 0.68-0.73) — the same methodology that grades the companion JME drug-resistance model. The only model for ASM withdrawal in JME. Note the withdrawal model rests on the 368 participants who actually attempted withdrawal, not the full 2518-person cohort.
calcs.rec_why: Editor's choice — the only model for ASM withdrawal in JME (tier A; IPD meta-analysis of 24 studies with internal-external cross-validation, c 0.70). Note it rests on the 368 people who attempted withdrawal, not the full 2518-person cohort.
